Article Title: ​A Broome woman's GP told her to bite off a lump on her tongue; she was later referred to a specialist by her dentist, who diagnosed tongue cancer, and surgery removed more than a third of her tongue
Article Text:
Her GP told her to bite it off

The cancer diagnosis

Why abnormal lumps should not be dismissed

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Monica Frain, a Broome resident, noticed a small lump on her tongue in late 2022. Her GP reportedly told her to bite it off, but a routine dental check-up changed the course of events. Her dentist flagged the growth and referred her to a specialist, who diagnosed tongue cancer, ABC News reported. Frain underwent five hours of surgery to remove more than a third of her tongue.Monica Frain first noticed a pinhead-sized lump on her tongue in late 2022. For months, the lump bothered her. In fact, she grew more annoyed than alarmed. She had recently undergone cardiac surgery and assumed that the lump could have been caused by the breathing tube placed during the procedure. She consulted a local general practitioner, who assured her there was nothing to worry about. In fact, the GP told her to bite the lump off.A routine dental examination flagged the growthAfter the GP's consultation, Monica Frain went for a routine dental check-up. Dentist Stephanie Mulcahy saw the lump and did not wait to see whether it would go away. She immediately referred Frain to an oral medicine specialist. "While it didn't look sinister, I wanted confirmation of what it was," Dr Mulcahy told the broadcaster.Getting a specialist opinion is difficult in Broome and across the Kimberley, the far north of Western Australia. Most specialists fly in from Perth, which is about 2,240 kilometres south, and work to a strict rotating schedule. Since Dr Mulcahy told her it wasn't ideal to wait, Frain flew to Perth in early 2023. She consulted an oral medicine specialist, who ordered a biopsy. The result showed squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). It is the most common form of tongue cancer, according to Cancer Research UK. Squamous cells are flat, skin-like cells that cover the lining of the mouth, nose, larynx, thyroid and throat. Since the cancer was detected early, it had not spread, and surgery was sufficient to treat it. However, the procedure still meant removing more than a third of her tongue. The surgery lasted five hours.Frain says she is ‘extremely grateful’ to Dr Mulcahy for her medical advice. "If Dr Steph had not pushed for me to go and see a specialist and have it removed, I could have been in a terrible state," she told the broadcaster.For Dr Mulcahy, though, it was simply part of her responsibility as a dentist to investigate anything that appeared unusual and ensure her patient received the right care. She has seen how these cancers can progress. She has identified tongue cancer in other patients, and one of them died of the disease.Oral and maxillofacial pathology specialist Omar Kujan told the broadcaster that Frain's case shows how much timing matters. "Regular dental check-ups can save lives by identifying early warning signs that people may not notice themselves," Dr Kujan said.The specialist also added that oral cancer can develop without pain or obvious symptoms. "Early diagnosis significantly improves the chances of successful treatment and survival. Timely access to oral healthcare must be a priority, particularly in regional and remote Australia."Tongue cancer is a type of head and neck cancer. Symptoms include a spot or lump on the tongue that does not go away. Smoking, alcohol consumption and infection with human papillomavirus (HPV) are some of the risk factors.
Article Summary: Monica Frain first noticed a pinhead-sized lump on her tongue in late 2022. Her GP told her to bite it off, but a routine dental check-up flagged the growth. She was referred to an oral medicine specialist, who ordered a biopsy. The result showed squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), the most common form of tongue cancer.

Article Title: An 82-year-old Arkansas man lived on his family's 331 acres for over 30 years, but relatives sought a sale; an appeals court later dismissed his challenge
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

A family inheritance became a property dispute

Why the court ordered the 331 acres sold

Appeals court dismisses the case as moot

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

An 82-year-old Arkansas man who had lived on his family's 331-acre property for more than three decades could not obtain a reversal of its court-ordered sale after the land was transferred to a third-party buyer. The dispute involved inherited property shared by relatives, with some family members seeking to sell the land while William J “Bud” Cooper wanted it divided among the co-owners so he could continue living there.In a November 18, 2026, decision available on Justia, the Arkansas Court of Appeals dismissed Cooper's appeal, ruling that the dispute had become moot because the property had already been sold and its title transferred. Although the majority did not decide the merits of his challenge to the partition order, two judges dissented, arguing that the lower court had committed reversible error and that Cooper had been deprived of his opportunity to obtain meaningful appellate review.The case concerned 331 acres near Boswell in Izard County, Arkansas. The property included pastureland, timberland, hills, creek and river-bottom areas, approximately 400 feet of frontage along the White River and seven platted town lots.The land originally belonged to Sylvester Smith, who died without a will in 1956. It subsequently passed to his three daughters. One daughter had no children, while the other two had descendants who became the Cooper and Bridgman families.By the time the legal dispute began, the Coopers collectively owned one-third of the property, while Stephanie Ann and Gary Alan Bridgman held the remaining two-thirds as tenants in common. In 2017, the Bridgmans filed a partition action seeking to have the property divided or sold if it could not be divided without substantial harm to the co-owners.Cooper and his sisters opposed the action. They claimed exclusive ownership through adverse possession and argued that the Bridgmans' long delay in seeking partition should prevent them from obtaining a sale under the legal doctrine of laches. Cooper also wanted the land divided physically rather than sold, allowing the family members to receive separate portions according to their ownership interests.After several hearings, the Izard County Circuit Court rejected the Coopers' claims of adverse possession and laches and granted the Bridgmans' partition petition. The court later rejected the Coopers' request for a division in kind, meaning a physical division of the land among the owners. Instead, it ordered an open-market sale through a real estate broker.However, the Arkansas Uniform Partition of Heirs Property Act requires a court to find that property cannot be divided in kind without great prejudice to the co-owners as a group before ordering a sale. The circuit court did not expressly make that required finding. The property was privately sold to a third party on February 5, 2025. The circuit court confirmed the sale on February 13 and subsequently authorised the distribution of the proceeds, with one-third going to the Coopers and two-thirds to the Bridgmans after outstanding debts were addressed.Cooper appealed the confirmation order, arguing that the court had failed to follow the statutory requirements before ordering the sale. He wanted the decision reversed and the case sent back for further proceedings to determine whether the land could be divided physically.The Arkansas Court of Appeals focused on what it could legally do after the sale had been completed. By the time the appeal was considered, the property had been transferred to a third-party purchaser who was not involved in the litigation. The court explained that it could not undo the transaction or return the land to Cooper.The majority therefore concluded that the appeal had become moot. It also noted that Cooper had not asked for monetary relief or challenged how the sale proceeds were divided. His requested remedy was to have the property returned for a possible physical division. Two judges, Barrett and Hixson, disagreed with the dismissal. In a dissenting opinion, Hixson argued that the circuit court had clearly failed to make the mandatory finding required under the Heirs Property Act before ordering a sale.He also criticised the appeals court for allowing the sale proceeds to be distributed while the appeal was pending and then dismissing the case because the dispute had become moot. He argued that the court could have reversed the decision and allowed the circuit court to consider whether another remedy was possible.The appeal was ultimately dismissed, leaving the completed sale undisturbed. The decision did not resolve whether the original partition order complied with the statutory requirements, but it highlighted the difficulties heirs can face when challenging the sale of inherited family property.
Article Summary: Arkansas Court of Appeals dismisses case as moot. Case involved inherited property shared by relatives. Some family members sought to sell the land, while others wanted to divide it. The court ordered an open-market sale through a real estate broker. By the time the appeal was considered, the property had been sold.

Article Title: A woman bought a £4,550 Cartier bracelet from Harrods but returned it because it was too small; the luxury retailer refused a refund, claiming she had scratched it, but a court ordered it to pay her £
Article Text:
Woman returns Cartier bracelet after finding it too small

Harrods claims bracelet had scratches and could not be resold

Judge questions Harrods' evidence over alleged scratches

Judge says she would happily take home supposedly worthless bracelet

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Harrods ordered to pay £5,131 to customer

A woman who spent £4,550 on a Cartier bracelet as a birthday treat has won a court battle against luxury department store Harrods after it refused to refund her money over allegations of damage. Georgia Romain, a hypnotherapist from Kingston upon Thames, London, had ordered the 18-carat gold bracelet online but decided to return it in July 2025 after finding that it was too small for her wrist. However, Harrods rejected the return, claiming that the jewellery had scratches and could no longer be resold. Romain challenged the retailer's evidence and eventually took the dispute to court without legal representation. The judge ruled in her favour, ordering Harrods to pay £5,131, including the original purchase price, interest and court fees.Romain had reportedly saved for years to purchase the Cartier Love bracelet, which she had planned as a birthday treat for herself. However, after receiving the 18-carat gold piece, she found that it was too small and did not fit her wrist properly.Having purchased it through Harrods' online store, she arranged to return the bracelet in its original box in July 2025, expecting a refund.The retailer subsequently informed her that the return had been rejected because the bracelet allegedly contained scratches and defects. Harrods also warned that the jewellery would be transferred to its lost property department unless she reclaimed it within 30 days.The decision left Romain without the bracelet or the money she had paid for it, prompting her to challenge the retailer's assessment of the returned item.The dispute centred on a pre-inspection video recorded by Harrods after receiving the returned bracelet. The retailer's customer service team used the footage to identify what it described as scratches and defects on the jewellery's soft gold surface.Harrods maintained that the bracelet had been damaged and argued that it could no longer be resold in that condition.However, Romain questioned whether the bracelet shown in the inspection footage was actually the one she had purchased. She pointed out that the video did not display the item's unique serial number and also suggested that the bracelet being examined appeared thicker than the one she had ordered.In an email to the retailer, she asked how she could be certain that the footage showed her bracelet without seeing its serial number. She requested evidence linking the alleged scratches to the specific item she had returned.According to the court proceedings, Harrods' subsequent response did not address her concerns about the missing serial number. Instead, the retailer formally rejected the return and informed her that the bracelet was legally her property.After failing to resolve the dispute with the retailer, Romain brought a claim against Harrods at London's Mayors and City County Court, representing herself without legal assistance.Deputy District Judge Elaine Vignoli ruled in her favour, finding that Harrods had failed to establish, on the balance of probabilities, that the bracelet was returned with the alleged scratches.The judge questioned why the retailer had not provided the evidence Romain had reasonably requested, particularly footage showing the bracelet's unique serial number alongside the alleged damage.She described Harrods' position in its email correspondence as "frankly staggering", noting that Romain had made a reasonable request concerning an item of considerable value.Harrods' lawyers argued that the bracelet would have been secured safely and handled carefully throughout the return process. However, the judge said there was no evidence before the court to substantiate that assurance.She concluded that the retailer had not proved that the scratches were present when it received the bracelet from Romain.The court also examined Harrods' argument that the alleged scratches had made the 18-carat gold bracelet worthless because it could no longer be resold.Judge Vignoli questioned this position, particularly because the retailer had not provided convincing evidence demonstrating how the alleged damage had affected the jewellery's value.In a pointed observation during the proceedings, she said: "If it is genuinely worthless I would happily take it home with me."The judge also described the bracelet as a "rather pretty, luxurious item" while discussing the retailer's claim that it had become worthless because of minor scuffs and scratches.She ultimately concluded that Harrods had failed to provide sufficient evidence to support its defence and ruled in favour of the customer.Following the ruling, Harrods was ordered to pay Romain £4,550, representing the original cost of the bracelet. With accumulated interest and court fees, the total amount payable came to £5,131.Romain described herself as "very relieved" after the outcome and said she would not shop at the luxury retailer again."I'm never buying from Harrods again," she said after the hearing.She also explained that she had spent years saving for the bracelet and had wanted to buy it as a special birthday present for herself."I was saving for years, I wanted to treat myself," she said, adding that she would return to saving money rather than making another expensive purchase.
Article Summary: Georgia Romain spent £4,550 on a Cartier Love bracelet for her birthday. She returned the 18-carat gold piece after finding it too small for her wrist. Harrods rejected the return, claiming the jewellery had scratches and could no longer be resold. Romain challenged the retailer's evidence and took the dispute to court. The judge ruled in her favour, ordering HarroDS to pay £5,131, including original purchase price, interest and court fees.

Article Title: A New Jersey boy was allegedly falsely blamed for a viral TikTok school shooting list, kept out of classes for over a year and bullied for years afterward; his parents have now sued school officials
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A New Jersey family has filed a lawsuit against a school district, accusing administrators of failing to protect their son after classmates allegedly falsely linked him to a viral TikTok school shooting threat. The student was kept away from school for more than a year and continued to face harassment after returning, according to a report by Daily Voice. The Ridgewood Blog also reported on the allegations, detailing the family’s claims that school officials treated the boy as a potential threat rather than addressing the bullying directed at him. The lawsuit was filed on November 5 in Bergen County Superior Court. It names the Ramsey Board of Education, Ramsey Borough School District, more than a dozen school officials, seven students and a parent as defendants. The student, identified in the complaint only as T.A., attended Eric S. Smith Middle School before moving on to Ramsey High School.According to the complaint, the situation began in January 2022, when a group of students allegedly spread rumours about T.A.‘s sexual orientation. Matters escalated when several students created an anonymous TikTok account featuring a list of students allegedly marked for killing on January 31, 2022.The account’s creators reportedly identified T.A. as the person behind the post, an accusation his family maintains was false. When T.A.‘s mother approached school administrators to report the allegations against her son, officials allegedly contacted the police instead. Officers subsequently arrived at the family’s home and took the boy to the Ramsey police station for questioning. He was released the same day, but the school reportedly informed his parents that he could not return to classes. The complaint states that T.A. remained on home instruction until March 2023, spending more than a year away from regular school attendance. The district allegedly classified the period as an out-of-school suspension.The allegations continued after his return to schoolReturning to the classroom did little to end the problems, according to the lawsuit. Students allegedly continued to associate T.A. with the TikTok threat, repeatedly questioning whether he owned weapons and suggesting that he intended to carry out an attack at school. One incident described in the complaint took place in October 2023 during a band class. A teacher allegedly expressed feeling threatened when T.A. was putting away a pair of scissors, while another student suggested that the boy might use them to stab someone.The accusations also reportedly affected the family’s life outside school. During the same month, a student and her mother allegedly told the family’s pastor that T.A. had been expelled and was stalking the student. The pastor subsequently asked the family to leave the church. According to the complaint, he later apologised and invited them back after learning about the accusations against the boy.The family further alleges that school administrators failed to respond appropriately to repeated complaints about harassment. In September 2024, Ramsey High School Principal Michael Thumm allegedly told T.A. and his parents to stop submitting harassment, intimidation and bullying complaints.The situation reportedly continued into 2026, with the complaint describing several additional accusations and physical incidents. In January, a student allegedly accused T.A. of rape, while another student claimed the following month that he was attempting to poison classmates using fentanyl-laced candy. Physical confrontations followed. In March 2026, a student allegedly punched T.A. in the stomach during an auto shop class while a teacher watched. The teacher reportedly responded by telling the student to watch his language. In June, another student allegedly slapped T.A. across the face, breaking his glasses.Family seeks damages over alleged school failuresThe lawsuit argues that school officials repeatedly failed to investigate complaints, address the alleged harassment or provide adequate protection. The family also maintains that T.A., who receives special education services, experienced significant physical and emotional harm as a result of the incidents. According to the complaint, the family has spent more than $3,600 on medical expenses related to the alleged injuries.The legal action includes claims of negligence, discrimination under New Jersey’s Law Against Discrimination, defamation, and intentional and negligent infliction of emotional distress, among other allegations. The family is seeking compensatory and punitive damages, reimbursement of attorney’s fees and a jury trial. However, the complaint does not specify the amount of compensation being sought.The case was filed by attorney Frederick E. Gerson of Feitlin, Youngman, Karas & Gerson LLC, based in Glen Rock, New Jersey. Ramsey Public Schools Superintendent Dr. Andrew C. Matteo said the district does not comment on pending litigation when approached by Daily Voice.
Article Summary: New Jersey family accuses school of failing to protect their son after classmates allegedly falsely linked him to a viral TikTok school shooting threat. The student was kept away from school for more than a year and continued to face harassment after returning, according to the lawsuit. The family is seeking compensatory and punitive damages.

Article Title: Forty years after California's Morongo tribe began sharing Thanksgiving food despite having little to spare, volunteers distributed 15,000 turkeys to 136 groups, taking their reported impact to nearly
Article Text:
Representative image of turkey from Canva

A tradition that began small

How the 2026 giveaway worked

California's Morongo tribe distributes 15,000 Thanksgiving turkeys, reaching 4.8 million mealsPhoto: Canva

Who is receiving help

Why the programme matters

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A legacy of giving

Forty years after California’s Morongo Band of Mission Indians began sharing Thanksgiving food despite having little to spare, volunteers distributed 15,000 turkeys to 136 groups this week, bringing the tribe’s reported impact to nearly 4.8 million meals. The annual giveaway, now in its 40th year, was reported by KESQ and NBC Palm Springs as a major regional effort to support families, seniors, and people experiencing homelessness during the holidays.The turkeys were distributed from the Morongo Community Center in Banning on November 16 and 17. They will help partner organisations prepare more than 300,000 Thanksgiving meals across the Inland Empire and neighbouring communities.The Morongo Band of Mission Indians started the Thanksgiving turkey giveaway in 1987, when the tribe had limited resources but believed that no one should go hungry during the holidays. Tribal Chairman Charles Martin said that belief has not changed.What began as a modest effort has grown into a large scale annual programme. Over four decades, the tribe says it has distributed nearly 245,000 turkeys and helped provide millions of holiday meals to people in need.This year’s 15,000 turkeys bring the reported total to nearly 4.8 million meals. The number reflects the cumulative impact of decades of giving, not just the current holiday season.Tribal members and volunteers gathered at the Morongo Community Center to sort and ship frozen turkeys to 136 organisations. The recipients include nonprofits, churches, and food pantries that will use the birds to prepare meals for their communities.The organisations receiving turkeys are based in Banning, Beaumont, Indio, Los Angeles, Mecca, Moreno Valley, Riverside, San Bernardino, and Temecula. Each group will use its allocation to prepare and serve meals to people who may otherwise go without a Thanksgiving dinner.The tribe begins accepting applications for turkey donations at the beginning of every year. Applications for the 2027 outreach programme are already available through the Morongo Nation website.The Coachella Valley Rescue Mission in Indio received 300 turkeys. Executive Director Amanda Galindo said the donation will help hundreds of men, women, and children who have nowhere else to go enjoy a Thanksgiving meal.The Galilee Center in Mecca also received 300 turkeys. The organisation will use them to support farmworkers, low income families, and seniors as it prepares for its own Thanksgiving food giveaway.Other recipients include Banning based Missionary Baptist Church, which received 100 turkeys, and the Janet Goeske Foundation in Riverside, which received 200. Both organisations plan to use the donations to prepare meals for families and seniors in need.For many recipients, the turkeys are more than food. They represent a chance to share a holiday meal with family, friends, or a community that may otherwise feel distant during the holidays.Caryn Chambers, executive board trustee at Missionary Baptist Church, said, as per the reports, that Morongo’s generosity is a blessing for Banning. She noted that the turkeys will help people enjoy a Thanksgiving dinner they might not have had otherwise.Danielle Stevens, executive director of the Janet Goeske Foundation, said that the holidays can be lonely for many seniors. She explained that a hot meal shared with friends can go a long way, and that Morongo helps make that happen.The 40 year milestone gives the programme a sense of continuity. It shows how a small act of generosity can grow into a lasting tradition that reaches thousands of people each year.The tribe’s approach has remained consistent. Rather than changing the mission, it has expanded the scale, adding more partners and more turkeys while keeping the focus on holiday meals.As the 2026 giveaway concludes, the programme is already looking ahead. Applications for 2027 are open, and the tribe says it will continue its effort to make sure more families have a meal to share during the holidays.
Article Summary: California's Morongo tribe distributes 15,000 Thanksgiving turkeys, reaching 4.8 million meals. The annual giveaway, now in its 40th year, was reported by KESQ and NBC Palm Springs. The recipients include nonprofits, churches, and food pantries that will use the birds to prepare meals for their communities.

A massive fire ripped through a commercial building on Thailand's southern resort island of Phuket early on Monday, killing at least 11 people and leaving 16 others injured, police told Reuters. The blaze broke out in the early hours of the morning and quickly spread to several nearby buildings, triggering a major firefighting operation.The fire erupted at around 3.17am local time (2017 GMT) at a shophouse housing a vehicle rental business. Article Title: GTA 6 release: Nearly 1 in 5 US workers plan to take time off to play
Article Text:
GTA 6 release: Nearly 1 in 5 US workers plan to take time off to play

Lander Allgood and Connor Folkers plan extended breaks for GTA 6 release

GTA flu: Why some gamers are planning to call in sick

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Nearly one in five salaried workers in the United States plans to take time off for the release of Grand Theft Auto 6 on Thursday, November 19. Some have already booked their paid leave, while others are considering calling in sick to spend the day playing the long-awaited game. A GameSquare survey also found that 36% of workers considering time off would rather call in sick than request leave. The trend, being called the ‘GTA flu’ online, comes after players waited 13 years for a new game in the popular franchise.For some players, the GTA 6 launch is worth planning their entire week around. Lander Allgood, a 26-year-old environmental specialist from the Dallas-Fort Worth area, requested two weeks of paid time off in July so he could enjoy the release.Allgood, who has played GTA 5 since he was around 13, compared the new game’s arrival to a major scientific achievement.“We’re basically witnessing, I mean, the Apollo space program of video games,” Allgood told USA TODAY.However, gaming is not his only responsibility. He plans to spend time with his two-year-old son and has arranged for his parents to look after the child from Thursday through Sunday. Once his son goes to bed, Allgood expects to spend hours playing.He is hoping to put in at least 20 hours over the weekend.Connor Folkers, a 22-year-old IT administrator from Iowa, has also arranged his schedule around the launch. He requested leave from November 19 through Thanksgiving and expects to spend more than 24 hours playing.For Folkers, getting enough time with the game before seeing other people’s reactions is important. He wants to experience the story and gameplay without online discussions shaping his opinion.“Really how I treat this game is sort of like a cultural event. You’re going to see this, I presume, everywhere online, whether it be story components or gameplay components, so I want to make sure I have enough time to really experience it for myself without the outside influencing my opinions on it,” Folkers told USA TODAY.He also compared the release to the Super Bowl, explaining how important the event has become for gaming enthusiasts.Not everyone is being upfront about taking a day off. Some players are planning to report sick on November 19 instead of requesting paid leave in advance.GameSquare surveyed 1,000 full-time US employees who identified as gamers. Its findings showed that 10% planned to skip work on launch day, while another 30% were considering taking time off. Among those considering leave, 36% said they would call in sick.BambooHR also found that nearly one in five salaried US workers planned to take time off for the release. Its figures showed that 32% of Gen Z employees and 27% of millennials intended to use paid leave to play.Nicole Csiszar, BambooHR’s director of HR, told USA TODAY that taking planned leave is a normal way for employees to enjoy their time away from work.“That’s a healthy sign,” Csiszar told USA TODAY. “It means people are using PTO the way it’s meant to be used, to step away and do something they enjoy.”She also pointed out why some might choose to call in sick instead.“Requesting PTO in advance means submitting it, waiting on approval and sometimes explaining why you want the day,” Csiszar told USA TODAY. “Calling in sick is one message that morning.”However, not every gamer is willing to put work aside. Ryan Van Dusen, a 42-year-old fifth-grade teacher from Michigan, has no plans to miss classes for the game. He is instead looking forward to playing during the Thanksgiving holiday.“My kids are expected to be in the classroom. I can’t take a day off from my students for this. This is preposterous,” Van Dusen told USA TODAY with a laugh. “In theory, Grand Theft Auto should be a small thing compared to work, family, things that are bigger. I think it’s healthy and good for us to have these small things that we can be excited for too and just to look forward to.”
Article Summary: Nearly one in five salaried workers in the United States plans to take time off for the release of Grand Theft Auto 6 on November 19. A GameSquare survey also found that 36% of workers considering time off would rather call in sick than request leave. The trend, being called the 'GTA flu' online, comes after players waited 13 years for a new game in the popular franchise.

Article Title: Watch: Fire outside MetLife Stadium sends smoke over field after Jets' 31-12 loss
Article Text:
Fire outside Met stadium

A fire broke out in an empty postgame tent outside MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on Sunday, sending thick clouds of smoke billowing over the venue hours after the New York Jets suffered their fifth consecutive defeat of the NFL season.Videos shared on social media showed large plumes of smoke rising near the stadium in East Rutherford and drifting over the playing field. One video also captured flames and black smoke erupting from the area near the venue.New Jersey State Police said troopers responded to a report of smoke shortly after 5:50 pm near Lot A and the stadium's American Express gate. They found a fire in an empty postgame tent, according to a report by Fox 5 New York.Fire crews brought the second-alarm blaze under control. No injuries or further damage were reported, while the cause of the fire was not immediately known.ESPN reporter Rich Cimini posted on social media that an announcement had been made inside the stadium about a “structure fire” near the adjacent train station. He later advised people to stay away from the stadium's east plaza, on the train station side, as smoke spread across the venue.Around 20 minutes later, he posted that the “situation has been resolved”.An NJ Transit spokesperson, quoted by NY Post said the fire did not disrupt train services in the area.The blaze broke out hours after the Jets lost 31-12 to the Buffalo Bills at MetLife Stadium. The defeat marked their fifth straight loss, leaving them with a 2-8 record for the season.The Jets struggled against the Bills, who secured a 19-point victory. The loss extended New York's losing streak and added to a difficult season for the team.
Article Summary: Fire broke out in an empty postgame tent outside MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on Sunday. The blaze sent thick clouds of smoke billowing over the venue hours after the New York Jets suffered their fifth consecutive defeat of the NFL season. No injuries or further damage were reported. The cause of the fire was not immediately known.

Article Title: 'He is my friend': Trump, Putin hold talks ahead of trilateral meeting with Xi on APEC sidelines
Article Text:
Trump Putin hold talks ahead of trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping

Trump-Putin meeting ahead of trilateral talks

Xi and Putin reaffirm strategic partnership

Putin criticises economic restrictions, calls for fairer world order

Nuclear arms control and Iran on trilateral agenda

US President Donald Trump held bilateral talks with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin, ahead of a trilateral discussion with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday.The meeting was held on the sidelines of APEC summit in Chinese city of Shenzhen.Trump expressed optimism ahead of the meeting"A lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start", he said."We will have a second meeting later on," he added.The meeting comes amid heightened diplomatic activity involving Washington, Moscow and Beijing, with the three leaders expected to discuss nuclear disarmament, the Iran conflict, the Russia-Ukraine war and global trade. The proposed trilateral engagement is being closely watched as a possible opportunity to address some of the most pressing geopolitical challenges.Trump arrived at the APEC venue earlier in the day, where he was welcomed by Xi. The US president subsequently met Putin, with the two leaders exchanging handshakes before joining other world leaders for a group photograph.The bilateral engagement between Trump and Putin comes a day after the Russian president held extensive discussions with Xi, reaffirming the strength of Moscow's strategic partnership with Beijing.The Trump-Putin meeting assumes importance as Washington and Moscow seek to address differences over the Ukraine war and the future of nuclear arms control.Trump had indicated before departing for Asia that the proposed discussions with Putin and Xi would cover several major international issues, including nuclear disarmament, Iran, Ukraine and economic relations."We're going to be talking about denuclearisation...We'll talk about Iran," Trump told reporters ahead of his departure.He also identified the Russia-Ukraine war as a key subject of discussion."We'll also talk about my favourite subject, Ukraine. Ukraine is losing. Ukraine and Russia are losing 25,000 souls per month, so we'll be talking about that. We'll also discuss economics and trade," Trump said.The proposed trilateral meeting would bring together the leaders of three major powers at a time when diplomatic efforts to resolve the Ukraine conflict have faced challenges.The prospect of discussions involving Washington and Moscow without Ukraine's direct participation has also raised concerns in Kyiv and among its European partners.Ahead of Trump's arrival, Xi and Putin held bilateral discussions in Shenzhen on Wednesday, reaffirming their commitment to strengthening economic, political and strategic cooperation.Xi described the relationship between China and Russia as resilient amid international uncertainty, saying their ties "stand as firm as a mountain amid wind and rain".He called on both countries to adopt a long-term strategic approach and shoulder greater responsibilities as major powers in shaping the international order."We must firmly shoulder the responsibilities expected of major powers, lead and advance the multipolarisation of the world and the democratisation of international relations," Xi said.Putin, meanwhile, described political cooperation between Moscow and Beijing as constructive despite the challenging international environment."Russian-Chinese political cooperation is working favourably and constructively in a difficult political situation," Putin stated."We are committed to constructive approaches to form a fairer multipolar world order," he added.The two leaders also discussed the need to expand cooperation across sectors, with Xi describing their partnership as a model of equality, mutual respect and mutually beneficial cooperation.According to Russian media reports, the discussions continued over a working breakfast in Shenzhen on Wednesday.Putin also addressed business representatives at the APEC CEO Summit, where he criticised the use of tariffs, sanctions and export restrictions as instruments of geopolitical and economic pressure.He argued that countries were increasingly seeking greater economic sovereignty and independence amid changes in the global geopolitical landscape."The regional model serves as a vivid example of strengthening a fairer, more democratic and equal world order," Putin said, referring to developments in the Asia-Pacific region.The Russian president criticised attempts by established economic powers to restrict the growth of emerging economies, arguing that such measures undermined fair competition and could ultimately hurt the countries imposing them.Putin acknowledged that tariffs, export restrictions and sanctions continued to affect economic development."But they are not capable of fully stopping growth or destroying the economies of the competition," he added.He also expressed expectations of "great use" from the proposed trilateral meeting involving Trump, Xi and himself.The proposed meeting comes at a sensitive moment for international nuclear arms control following the expiration of the New START treaty between the United States and Russia in February 2026.Trump has expressed interest in negotiating a new nuclear arms control framework that would include China alongside Washington and Moscow.However, Beijing has traditionally resisted joining such negotiations, pointing to the considerably larger nuclear arsenals maintained by the United States and Russia.The Iran conflict is another issue expected to feature in the discussions, alongside disagreements over international trade, tariffs, technology restrictions and global supply chains.China has described the proposed trilateral engagement as being of "ground-breaking significance", with the potential to safeguard global peace and promote strategic stability among major powers.The APEC summit has consequently emerged as an important diplomatic platform for Washington, Moscow and Beijing to engage on issues ranging from nuclear security to regional conflicts and the future of the global economic order.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump held bilateral talks with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin, ahead of a trilateral discussion with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The meeting was held on the sidelines of APEC summit in Chinese city of Shenzhen. The proposed trilateral engagement is being closely watched as a possible opportunity to address some of the most pressing geopolitical challenges.

US president Donald Trump on Thursday opposed international efforts to regulate or restrict the development of superintelligence (SI), saying Washington would not allow measures that could stifle the technology.Addressing the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen, China, he described SI as the biggest technological transformation since the Industrial Revolution.“The United States is also proud to be the world leader in superintelligence, SI, the greatest technological transformation since the Industrial Revolution. Americans invented—we just invented SI, and it is unleashing extraordinary prosperity and growth for people all around the globe,” Trump said.While promoting the technology’s potential, Trump acknowledged that its development could carry risks and called for safeguards to manage them.“We have to watch it. We have to be careful. We have to cherish it. It's almost completely good, but it's got some bad elements, so we have to be very careful in managing those bad elements,” he said.However, he ruled out global regulatory measures, arguing that they could impede innovation.“So we oppose any form of globalist regulation or anything to control or stifle SI, and we won't allow that to happen, frankly,” Trump added.Trump also used the address to highlight his administration’s economic record, claiming that inflation had remained below two per cent over the preceding three months.“The last 3 months, inflation was down to a number that was not expected. We were able to do a real job. You know, a lot of other countries are having difficulty with that, but we've gotten it less than 2% for the last 3 months,” he said.He claimed the US had secured commitments worth $22.2 trillion in new investments and generated $25 trillion in new wealth up to November 1. Article Title: Scientists tracked Manx shearwaters across the Atlantic for two decades and found that fast eastward flights can give birds jet lag; even experienced adults drift off course before correcting their ro
Article Text:
Manx Shearwaters, the marine birds that hunt over the open ocean Image credits: Oxford University

How a slow body clock sends birds the wrong way

Infographic showing clock-shift that occurs during homing flights of shearwaters. The bird begins to home at point A. On the first day of homing, its endogenous clock is calibrated to local time at 30°W. However, the shearwater travels eastwards to 15°W over 6 hours to point B. Here, sunrise happened an hour earlier, so the shearwater’s perceived time lags local time by an hour and the sun is roughly 20° further clockwise than the shearwater expects. At point B, this discrepancy causes the shearwater to orient roughly 20° clockwise of the correct direction. Image Credits: Credit: Lewin et al, 2026. Oxford University

Small errors for adults, bigger risks for first-timers

Manx shearwater in flight over sea Image credits: thelonekayaker/ wordpress

Manx Shearwater Puffinus puffinus Image credits: birdsoftheworld.org
