Manx shearwaters flying home from feeding trips can be nudged off course by a kind of jet lag, researchers say. It happens when a bird’s body clock falls out of step with the local time. Tracking data from Manx shearwaters on the west coast of the UK revealed that when the birds returned home to their colonies after trips over the Atlantic, their rapid eastward flights disrupted their sense of time and navigation.When humans get jet lag, we fly across time zones and feel tired and out of sync because our body clock is still running on the old time. Shearwaters seem to have a similar problem. For them, it shows up as a wrong turn over the open sea.A studyfinds that long-distance flights can throw seabirds' internal clocks out of sync, causing navigation errors , it was published in October 2026 on the Oxford University website. It talks about how researchers in Oxford University's Department of Biology analysed 20 years of GPS tracking data from 1,045 breeding shearwaters, covering 3,688 foraging trips. The birds set off from colonies on the west coasts of the UK and Ireland. Some flew about 1,000km west to find food. On the way home, they flew east, back to their nests.Like many animals, shearwaters use the sun as a compass. This is very useful over open water, where there are no roads or landmarks. But the sun moves across the sky during the day, so a bird needs to know the time to work out where the sun should be. The bird’s body clock gives it that information. It is called the circadian rhythm. Birds normally reset their clocks at sunrise. That works well while a bird stays in one place. But when a bird travels quickly east or west, its clock can fall out of sync with local solar time. On the flight home, the shearwaters crossed places where the sun rises earlier. The Oxford release says this can leave their clocks lagging behind local time by up to around one hour.The researchers worked out how a slow clock should change the birds’ sun compass. Then they compared those predictions with the directions the GPS trackers recorded. As the birds travelled east, they tended to drift clockwise from their expected direction. That is what you would expect if their clocks were running behind. The team from the Department of Biology found that when the predicted compass error pointed towards land, the shearwaters flew closer to the coast. When it pointed away from land, they flew further out to sea. So the birds seem to use the sun compass even when familiar land is close by.The errors were real, but they were small. In “Seabirds get jet lag, too — and it can throw them a bit off course,” published by Science News on October 29, 2026, Anirban Mukhopadhyay reports that the birds veered by as much as 15 degrees. The errors were small enough to add only a few kilometres to the journey. They were not enough to stop the shearwaters from finding their way home.Adult birds can fix their mistakes because they keep checking where they are. The Oxford team calculated that a shearwater returning from 1,000 km away with an average compass error of seven degrees would fly only about 5 km further than needed to get within 5 km of its colony.“It’s inherently difficult to study the cognitive processes of animals in the wild, so it’s exciting to realise that if we measure their natural movements carefully enough we can reveal the underlying behavioural mechanisms.” - Co-author Professor Tim Guilford, Department of Biology, Oxford University. The consequences could be more significant for animals that cannot continuously reassess and correct their positions.For example, young birds undertaking their first migration could be particularly vulnerable. Small navigational errors might accumulate over a long journey, potentially shifting their eventual destination by hundreds of kilometres.Researchers do not yet know whether the clock mismatch affects the birds in other ways. Internal clocks control many parts of an animal’s behaviour and body, so the problem could reach beyond navigation. More work is needed to find out. Dr Patrick Lewin, the lead researcher, has said that studying animals that regularly travel long distances could one day help us understand how humans cope with jet lag. “It’s amazing to think that billions of migratory animals look up to the sun for direction, relying on clocks silently ticking away inside them, and that errors in those clocks can cause them to take tiny shifts off course. ” - Lead researcher Dr Patrick Lewin, Department of Biology, Oxford University.
Article Summary: Manx shearwaters flying home from feeding trips can be nudged off course by a kind of jet lag, researchers say. It happens when a bird’s body clock falls out of step with the local time. For them, it shows up as a wrong turn over the open sea.

Article Title: The grand optics of Xi-Trump-Putin meet; why the talks may not be a game changer
Article Text:
Russian President Vladimir Putin, left, Chinese President Xi Jinping, center, and U.S. President Donald Trump attend a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa in Shenzhen, southern China's Guangdong province, Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. (Sergei Bobylev/Sputnik, Kremlin Pool Photo via AP)

Why the Yalta comparison does not hold

AI and technology competition could limit cooperation

Nuclear arms control: A difficult area for consensus

Trade, energy and supply chains offer limited common ground

Europe and India concerned about being left out

Why a major breakthrough is unlikely

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The first-ever trilateral meeting between US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin has brought three of the world's most powerful leaders together at a time of deep geopolitical divisions. Held on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen on November 19, the meeting carries considerable diplomatic and political symbolism. However, despite the grand optics, expectations of a major breakthrough on issues such as the Ukraine war, nuclear arms control, artificial intelligence and global trade remain limited.The meeting lasted around 90 minutes, shortly after which the Kremlin said it was "difficult to say whether the trilateral format had a future".The optics of the gathering are important in themselves. Trump has presented dialogue with leaders with whom the US has disagreements as an alternative to avoiding engagement. Putin, meanwhile, gets an opportunity to challenge the perception of Russia's diplomatic isolation following the Ukraine war. Xi's participation reinforces China's position as a major player in discussions on the international order.Also read - 'Chaos if major powers clash': Xi's warning at trilateral with Trump, Putin - who said what JNU professor Dr Rajan Kumar, in a conversation with The Times of India, said the meeting's importance lies primarily in the political and diplomatic weight of the three leaders. He also explained why comparisons with the Yalta Conference of 1945 may be misplaced and why the summit is unlikely to fundamentally alter the global order.The meeting has drawn comparisons with the Yalta Conference, an eight-day meeting held near Yalta in Crimea in February 1945, during World War II. US President Franklin D Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met to discuss the post-war settlement in Europe. The conference helped shape the arrangements for defeated Germany, including its division into occupation zones, and influenced the emerging political order in Europe.Explaining the significance of the present gathering, Kumar said, "The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum was established in the late 1980s, primarily to promote regional stability and economic growth in the Asia-Pacific region. Its formation was aimed at strengthening economic cooperation and ensuring stability in the post-Cold War political environment. At that time, the United States maintained good relations with China, Japan, South Korea and other countries in the region. The objective was to create a framework that would support regional stability and economic development."He said the geopolitical context had changed since then, adding, "However, the global situation has changed considerably since then. The current meeting has become important because three of the world's most influential leaders are coming together. Some commentators have compared it to the Yalta Conference of 1945. The comparison is largely because Donald Trump is the leader of the world's most powerful military power, Xi Jinping heads the world's second-most powerful country, and Russia remains one of the most important military powers globally. Their coming together therefore carries considerable political and symbolic significance."The comparison has raised concerns that the three leaders could discuss the future of Ukraine and European security without the participation of the countries directly affected by their decisions. European countries, in particular, fear that an understanding among Washington, Moscow and Beijing could influence the continent's security architecture.Kumar said the political messaging behind the meeting was also important. "There is also a political messaging aspect to this meeting. Trump has faced domestic political setbacks following the midterm elections and wants to project himself as a leader who can work with powerful world leaders. For Putin, the meeting offers an opportunity to counter Russia's diplomatic isolation by the West. At the same time, the absence of Europe and India from this engagement has raised concerns that major decisions affecting their security interests could be discussed without their participation. "Referring to the concerns over a possible understanding on Ukraine, he said, "European countries, in particular, are concerned about the possibility of an understanding between the three leaders that could affect Ukraine and the wider European security architecture. Some have drawn parallels with the Yalta Conference, where Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin agreed on arrangements for post-war Europe, including the division of Germany into different zones. There are fears that a similar understanding could emerge over Ukraine or European security."However, Kumar said the Yalta comparison was not valid because the circumstances surrounding the two meetings were fundamentally different."In my view, this comparison is not particularly valid. It is like comparing apples with oranges. At Yalta, the Allied powers had won the war and were in a position to impose terms and arrangements on defeated countries such as Germany and Japan. In the present situation, neither Russia has won the war against Ukraine nor has the United States won the war against Iran. Both conflicts remain unresolved. Therefore, the circumstances are fundamentally different, and this meeting is unlikely to produce consequences of the same magnitude," he said.Also read: Watch: On way to meet Putin, Trump lends helping hand to Xi Jinping on escalator Artificial intelligence is one of the major issues that could feature in discussions among the three countries. Establishing common rules and regulatory frameworks could be an area of cooperation, but the technology rivalry between Washington and Beijing makes consensus difficult.Asked what could emerge from the meeting, Kumar said, "There are two or three major issues that could be discussed, particularly those relating to global governance. One important issue is artificial intelligence. If the three countries can discuss common rules, laws and regulatory frameworks for AI, it could be considered an achievement. At present, the United States has its own policy, China has a different approach, and other countries are developing their own regulations. "He said Washington's priority was to retain its technological lead and prevent China from catching up. "However, the United States' broader policy is aimed at maintaining its dominance in artificial intelligence and preventing China from catching up. Trump believes that the US should retain its technological lead. At the same time, China is making efforts to develop its own advanced chips and technology networks. The United States may continue supplying certain technologies to China while ensuring that China does not emerge as the world's leading producer and supplier of advanced chips. The objective is to keep China dependent on certain technologies while maintaining American dominance in the AI sector."This competition, Kumar said, would make it difficult for the two countries to agree on common regulations. "This competition makes it difficult for the two countries to agree on common regulations. Each fears that restrictions could affect its own companies while allowing the other country to gain a competitive advantage. Therefore, reaching a consensus on AI governance will be challenging."Nuclear arms control is another major issue that could be discussed at the summit. The US and Russia have a long history of negotiating agreements to limit and regulate their nuclear arsenals. Agreements such as SALT, the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty (INF), START and New START formed part of the framework governing strategic competition between Washington and Moscow. China, however, has not been part of these bilateral arrangements.Kumar said bringing Beijing into a future nuclear arms control agreement would be difficult because of the disparity between the countries' arsenals."The second major issue is nuclear disarmament. Until now, most nuclear arms agreements, including SALT, INF, START and New START, have been negotiated between the United States and the Soviet Union or Russia. China has never been part of these arrangements. Trump may raise the possibility of including China in a future nuclear arms agreement, but Beijing is likely to remain reluctant," he said.Explaining China's position, he added, "China believes there is no reason for it to accept the same restrictions as the United States and Russia because its nuclear arsenal is much smaller. China is estimated to possess around 600 nuclear warheads, compared with approximately 5,000 or more in the American and Russian arsenals. There is no parity between the three countries, which makes Beijing's participation in a nuclear arms control agreement difficult. "The difference in nuclear capabilities is likely to remain a major obstacle to any trilateral arrangement. While discussions could help establish communication, a comprehensive agreement would require all three countries to agree on terms that address their respective security concerns.Energy security and global supply chains could provide another area for discussion. Unlike nuclear arms control and AI, these issues may offer some scope for cooperation without requiring the three countries to resolve their wider geopolitical differences.Kumar said, "Energy security and supply chains could be another area of discussion where some understanding may be possible. However, I do not believe these leaders are in a position to fundamentally change the course of the world order through this meeting."He also pointed to the diplomatic symbolism surrounding the leaders' interactions. "Beyond the political messaging and symbolism, the leaders have met warmly. Xi personally received Trump at the airport, while a different protocol arrangement was followed for Putin. This indicates the importance Trump is attaching to China despite the controversies and tensions that have emerged in recent days."A joint statement or an understanding on specific issues could be an outcome of the meeting, but Kumar said even that would be difficult to achieve. "If the meeting produces some substantive discussions, a consensus on certain issues or a joint statement, that itself would be an achievement. However, I consider such an outcome unlikely."The absence of Europe and India from the trilateral engagement has raised questions about their role in discussions that could affect their strategic interests. European countries remain particularly concerned about the future of Ukraine and the wider security architecture of the continent. India, meanwhile, has important diplomatic, economic and security relationships with all three powers.Kumar said the concern was particularly strong among countries that could be affected by any understanding reached by the three leaders."The fear of being left out is particularly strong among European countries and India. They are concerned that an understanding between the three major powers could influence their security architecture without their participation. European countries are especially worried about decisions that could affect Ukraine and the future of European security," he said.Ukraine, in particular, could face pressure to consider negotiations. However, the participation of the three major powers does not mean they can impose a settlement on Kyiv.Kumar said, "Ukraine is currently in a difficult position, and the three leaders could potentially exert pressure on Kyiv. However, the situation does not allow for a straightforward settlement imposed by the major powers."Despite the political significance of the gathering, expectations of a major agreement should remain limited. The three countries have competing strategic priorities, and their leaders are unlikely to make commitments that could compromise their national interests.Kumar does not expect the meeting to produce a major breakthrough. "I do not expect anything very substantive to emerge from this meeting. All three leaders are important, and their coming together at a time of global conflicts, geopolitical tensions and ideological differences is itself noteworthy. However, the expectations of a major agreement should remain limited," he said.He also pointed to the uncertainty surrounding Trump's approach to international negotiations. "Trump is not viewed by the other leaders as an entirely predictable negotiating partner. They understand that his policies and decisions can change quickly. Their approach is therefore likely to be to maintain stable relations with Washington and avoid decisions that could adversely affect their countries."Kumar concluded that the meeting's value would largely remain symbolic and political rather than mark a shift in the global order."The meeting may have considerable symbolic and political value, but it is unlikely to produce a major agreement that changes the existing global order."
Article Summary: The first-ever trilateral meeting between US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin has brought three of the world's most powerful leaders together. JNU professor Dr Rajan Kumar said the meeting's importance lies primarily in the political and diplomatic weight of the three leaders. He also explained why comparisons with the Yalta Conference of 1945 may be misplaced and why the summit is unlikely to fundamentally alter the global order.

Article Title: A Texas college student and her father missed connecting flights and failed to secure permits for Zion National Park’s Angels Landing hike; strangers then offered spare permits, saving their dream tri
Article Text:
Flight delays put the trip in jeopardy

An unsuccessful permit application

A small favour led to an unexpected opportunity

A challenging climb and an unforgettable experience

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Strangers turned into friends

A father-daughter getaway to Utah nearly ended in disappointment after flight delays and an unsuccessful permit application threatened to derail their plans to hike one of America’s most famous trails. But an unexpected encounter with fellow hikers at Zion National Park changed everything. Jordan Phillips, a college student from Texas, and her father, Brent, eventually got their chance to tackle Angels Landing after meeting a group of strangers who offered them two unused permit spots. Their experience was reported by KSL News and subsequently picked up by other outlets, including Hoodline. Scroll down to read more.The pair had just one weekend to make the journey worthwhile. However, their travel plans began falling apart when their flight was delayed, causing them to miss a connecting flight in Denver. Their replacement flight was also delayed multiple times, leaving them uncertain about whether they would reach Utah in time.Despite the setbacks, Jordan remained grateful for the opportunity to spend time with her father.Brent, meanwhile, was determined to make the trip happen. Once they finally arrived in Utah, however, another obstacle emerged. Their application for Angels Landing permits had been unsuccessful.Angels Landing is among the most recognisable hiking destinations in Zion National Park, famous for its dramatic canyon views, steep climbs and exposed ridgeline. Its final section involves a narrow trail with metal chains that hikers hold on to while navigating steep drop-offs.Because of the route’s popularity and safety concerns, the National Park Service introduced a permit system in 2022. Visitors must secure a permit through either a seasonal lottery or a day-before lottery to hike the section between Scout Lookout and the summit. Jordan and Brent had applied but failed to secure places. They approached a park ranger to ask whether anything could be done, but were told they could not proceed without the required permits. The pair decided to follow the ranger’s suggestion and explore another trail instead.Their plans took an unexpected turn when they encountered a woman hiking alone. The father and daughter offered to take her photograph before continuing along the trail. Later, they came across the same woman again, this time accompanied by her hiking friends. The two groups began talking, and the conversation eventually turned to Angels Landing.The hikers had two unused places available, which they offered to Jordan and Brent, according to KSL’s account. The unexpected opportunity meant the father and daughter could finally attempt the hike they had travelled so far to experience.There is one important detail about the permit arrangement: National Park Service rules state that Angels Landing permits are non-transferable and that the size of an awarded group cannot be increased. KSL’s report does not explain how the pair were formally included in the group’s permit arrangements.For Brent, accepting the opportunity meant confronting something he was not particularly comfortable with: heights. He admitted that he was not properly dressed for the hike and had brought unsuitable footwear. Nevertheless, he decided to accompany his daughter and take on the challenging route.Jordan was particularly touched by her father’s willingness to push through his discomfort. For her, the experience was about more than reaching the summit. It was also a reminder of how far her father was willing to go to make her happy.The climb eventually rewarded them with sweeping views of Zion Canyon. Rain began falling as they reached the top, adding another unexpected element to an already memorable adventure. The pair also spent time with the group who had helped them, sharing stories and enjoying the experience together.Looking back on the weekend, Jordan and Brent said the people they encountered had become just as important to the experience as the hike itself. The encounter reinforced their belief that striking up conversations with strangers can lead to meaningful connections. Jordan hopes their experience encourages other travellers to be more open to meeting people along the way.The trip also changed Brent’s attitude towards hiking. Although he had initially been reluctant to take on the strenuous trail, he returned home with a different outlook and an interest in planning more outdoor adventures with his daughter. What began as a weekend threatened by missed flights and rejected permits ultimately became a shared experience the two are already looking forward to repeating.
Article Summary: Jordan Phillips, a college student from Texas, and her father, Brent, eventually got their chance to tackle Angels Landing. The pair had just one weekend to make the journey worthwhile. Their travel plans began falling apart when their flight was delayed, causing them to miss a connecting flight in Denver.

Article Title: Indian-origin Samit Patel charged with attempted murder after strangling Uber driver, crushing him with car in Minnesota
Article Text:
Samit Apurva Patel/Image: AP

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

An Indian-origin man has been charged with attempted murder and carjacking in Minnesota after allegedly attacking an Uber driver, strangling him with a seatbelt and running him over with his own vehicle.Samit Apurva Patel, 25, who lives in Hopkins, faces charges of attempted second-degree murder and first-degree carjacking following the Saturday assault on Mohamed Yusuf, 51. He is being held on $1 million bail, according to a criminal complaint filed in Hennepin County District Court.The incident occurred shortly before 1 am in Hopkins, a suburb of Minneapolis. Yusuf was on a phone call with his brother, who also works as an Uber driver, when he picked up Patel, court documents said.The brother allegedly heard the passenger tell Yusuf that he did not like his name, Mohamed, CBS News reported.As per the complaint, Patel used a seatbelt to strangle Yusuf before taking control of the vehicle. Yusuf was then run over and left in a ditch. Police believe the vehicle may have returned to the scene and struck him a second time.Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty announced the charges on Tuesday, describing the incident as an “incredibly brutal attack”.Yusuf sustained multiple serious injuries, including broken ribs, a fractured leg, spinal damage, collapsed lungs and extensive internal bleeding. The complaint states that several of his organs had to be removed.His family said he has undergone several operations and remains in a coma at Hennepin County Medical Centre in Minneapolis. His son, Mustafa Osman, said the family was struggling to deal with the extent of his father's injuries.Relatives believe the assault was driven by hatred, prompting calls from civil rights advocates for authorities to investigate it as a possible hate crime.However, Moriarty said prosecutors could not establish the required evidence to bring a bias-related charge. Under Minnesota law, authorities must demonstrate that a crime was deliberately motivated by prejudice against a protected characteristic.“We cannot criminally charge someone who may hold biased beliefs …. We must be able to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the criminal act was motivated by those biased beliefs,” Moriarty said, according to KSTP.She added that the decision not to pursue a hate crime charge did not lessen the suffering of Yusuf's family or the wider Somali community.Yusuf had worked as a taxi and ride-hailing driver for several years. His family described him as a dedicated father who was known for his empathy and ability to calm difficult situations.The attack has also raised concerns among Minnesota's Somali-American community, the largest Somali population in the United States, with many residents based in the Minneapolis-St Paul metropolitan area.
Article Summary: Samit Apurva Patel, 25, faces charges of attempted second-degree murder and first-degree carjacking following the Saturday assault on Mohamed Yusuf, 51. Yusuf sustained multiple serious injuries, including broken ribs, a fractured leg, spinal damage, collapsed lungs and extensive internal bleeding. Patel is being held on $1 million bail.

Article Title: A 58-year-old grandmother thought the cross she dug up in a British field after five fruitless hours was costume jewellery, but it was a medieval gold reliquary that could be worth up to £20,000
Article Text:
The medieval gold cross features Jesus' crucifixion on one side and Mary holding Jesus on the other.

After five hours of searching, I found something remarkable

Historical importance of medieval artifact

British Museum to assess cross

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A British grandmother's routine day of metal detecting turned into a centuries-old discovery after she stumbled upon a small gold cross buried beneath a farmer's field after hours of searching. She dismissed the object as cheap costume jewelry at first, not realizing that the tiny artifact was a medieval treasure that could be worth as much as £20,000. The surprise find has since drawn attention to its historical significance and could also bring a financial reward for the hobbyist.According to Parade and Newsbreak, the find was made in August by 58-year-old Shelley Couzins, a grandmother of five, on the Isle of Sheppey in Kent, England. Couzins, who has been into metal detecting for about four years, was out exploring a freshly plowed farmer's field with other members of the Medway History Finders group.The search began without much hope, as the grandmother is said to have found only undesirable metal objects all morning. After five hours or so of finding nothing of much value, her detector finally signaled something buried underground around lunchtime.She dug in the dirt, about 12 inches and found a small cross. The object initially looked like normal jewelry and she thought it was a costume piece rather than something of historical importance. But her understanding of the discovery changed rapidly when fellow metal-detecting enthusiasts at the group's main tent reacted. Then they realized the cross was made of solid gold. What they thought was an ordinary find was going to be a potentially valuable historical artifact.Parade and Newsbreak reported that the object was quickly identified as a medieval gold reliquary cross. The artifact weighs about 10.6 grams and has two religious images on it. On one side is the crucifixion of Jesus Christ, on the other Mary holding Jesus. The find is especially significant because of its complex religious imagery and gold composition.Couzins was lucky, too, that the object survived intact. Newsbreak reported that she was relieved to find the cross undamaged, as another pass of the agricultural plow could potentially have struck and broken it. The investigating team has kept the exact location of the find secret out of fears that publicity could bring illegal treasure hunters.While there's excitement about the discovery, Couzins can't just take the medieval cross home. Under Britain's treasure laws, qualifying archeological discoveries have to be reported to the relevant authorities. Having been identified and assessed the object was passed to a Finds Liaison Officer. Now the British Museum is examining the artifact and will decide if it wants to acquire it for its collection.Newsbreak says it has been valued at about £20,000 – or about $27,000. This figure is not an official valuation, however, and remains subject to the judgment of the museum.If the British Museum decides to keep the cross, an official monetary valuation will be placed on it. The money would then be split between Couzins and the land owner leaving the grandmother with a nice financial windfall.Image Courtesy: Google Gemini
Article Summary: Shelley Couzins, 58, found a small gold cross buried beneath a farmer's field. She dismissed the object as cheap costume jewelry at first, not realizing that the tiny artifact was a medieval treasure that could be worth as much as £20,000. The British Museum is examining the artifact and will decide if it wants to acquire it for its collection.

Article Title: US lawmakers want Trump to press Xi over wrongfully detained Americans, political prisoners
Article Text:
US lawmakers urge Trump to raise wrongfully detained americans, political prisoners with Xi Jinping

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Senior US lawmakers have urged President Donald Trump to raise the cases of wrongfully detained American citizens and other political prisoners with Chinese President Xi Jinping during their scheduled meeting in Shenzhen on Thursday.The appeal was made by House Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar, Values Action Team Chairman Robert B Aderholt and Congressional-Executive Commission on China (CECC) Co-Chairman Chris Smith, according to a press release issued by the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party (CCP).The lawmakers urged the Trump administration to make the release of people detained on political grounds a priority in its talks with Beijing.They cited the release of Pastor Ezra Jin in July as an example of successful diplomatic engagement by the Trump administration. However, they said several other religious leaders, activists, journalists and prisoners of conscience continued to remain behind bars in China.In a joint statement, the lawmakers said that freedom of religion, speech and association were universal rights, but accused the Chinese Communist Party of continuing to deny these freedoms to innocent people.They pointed to the case of Pastor Ezra Jin, who spent nearly nine months in prison for leading a church. While he has been released, several other pastors, religious believers and journalists remain imprisoned, they said.The lawmakers also raised concerns over the imprisonment of Hong Kong pro-democracy media tycoon Jimmy Lai, 78, who was sentenced to 20 years in prison for his role in running the newspaper Apple Daily. They described the sentence as effectively a death sentence for a man of his age and said the American people had not forgotten his case.They also highlighted the case of pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong, who turned 30 while in prison and was recently handed an additional 10-year sentence. The lawmakers said they would continue to push for the release of both Lai and Wong.The statement also called for the immediate release of two American citizens, Youlin Chen and Min Zin, whom the lawmakers described as "wrongfully detained" scholars. They were arrested on allegations of endangering China's national security while conducting academic research.Other prisoners of conscience mentioned in the statement included Gulshan Abbas, a retired Uyghur physician; Christian pastor Gao Quanfu and his wife Pang Yu; members of Pastor Ezra Jin's Beijing Zion Church; and Uyghur scholar Ilham Tohti.According to the press release, Gulshan Abbas went missing in September 2018, days after her sister and Uyghur rights advocate Rushan Abbas publicly spoke about the persecution of Uyghurs. The lawmakers called for her release.They also raised the cases of Pastor Gao Quanfu and his wife Pang Yu, who remain detained over their Christian faith. Members of Beijing Zion Church are also behind bars following the October 2025 crackdown in which Pastor Ezra Jin was arrested.The lawmakers further highlighted the case of Ilham Tohti, a Uyghur academic who received the European Parliament's Sakharov Prize in absentia in 2019. He has remained in prison since his arrest and life sentence in 2014, the press release said.The Select Committee on the CCP also noted that both the US House of Representatives and Senate had passed resolutions calling for the release of American citizens wrongfully detained in China and other prisoners of conscience.The lawmakers reiterated their appeal to Trump to raise these cases directly with Xi and press for the release of those detained on political and religious grounds. They said the freedom and welfare of prisoners of conscience should remain a key priority in US engagement with China.
Article Summary: US lawmakers urge Trump to raise wrongfully detained americans, political prisoners with Xi Jinping. The appeal was made by House Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar, Values Action Team Chairman Robert B Aderholt and Congressional-Executive Commission on China (CECC) Co-Chairman Chris Smith.

Article Title: Landsat images show Utah’s Cottonwood Fire turning green mountain terrain into a burn scar; by July 7, it had burned about 150 square miles
Article Text:
Landsat images from 5 June and 29 June 2026 show the same Utah mountains before and after the Cottonwood fire. Image Credits: NASA

A dry season and a risky forecast

How fast the fire grew

The Cottonwood fire burning in Utah on 24 June 2026, one day after NASA data showed it tripling in size. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons

What burned and what survived

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Where climate comes into play

Two satellite images taken 24 days apart tell a worrying story. According to NASA's Earth Observatory , Landsat 8 and Landsat 9 satellites took images of the same section of Utah on 5 June and 29 June 2026. In these false-colour images, unburned vegetation appears bright green. The first image is of mountains that hadn’t been burned yet. The second shows a large brown scar across most of the picture. By 7 July, the Cottonwood Fire had burned about 150 square miles (390 square kilometres). NASA describes it as having been among the largest and most destructive fires in Utah and the nation up to that point in 2026.The land was ready to burn. NASA notes that the winter saw below-average snowpack, while the start of summer was unusually warm and dry. The National Interagency Fire Center had warned that the Great Basin region and portions of the Rocky Mountains faced an increased threat of wildfire in July. On 7 July, firefighters were fighting nearly three dozen large early-season fires in the Western US. Among those, Utah stood out with 558 square miles burned across all its fires. Nationwide, the fires had already burned 5,265 square miles of territory. That's 46% more than the 10-year average for that point in the season.In terms of size, the Cottonwood Fire fell just shy of the Babylon Fire of eastern Utah.The Cottonwood Fire grew very fast as well. NASA's Fire Events Data Suite uses three satellites with heat-detecting sensors. It showed the fire spreading north, east, and south, tripling in size over 12 hours on 23 June. On 26 June, it made another run to the north. University of Maryland scientist Tempest McCabe, who helped develop the tool, says it delivers consistent, easily accessible data that doesn't need to be specifically requested. That helps it often spot the start of a fire sooner than other sources. On 7 July, the fire was 56% contained with 1,289 firefighters on the ground. Forecasters expected hot, dry weather to continue.Among the vegetation destroyed by the fire are ponderosa pine, oak, sagebrush and grass. Officials with the state's forestry division told news media that the fire had destroyed about 150 buildings. The Eagle Point Ski Resort lost over 100 condos and 30 cabins, and it reported damage to four out of the five chairlifts. However, some patches of green managed to survive, like the forests near the Tushar Campground, which hosts a 4-H summer camp. Beaver County officials credited forest work like clearing the brush and trimming branches with helping save the campground and nearby forests.Research supports the general idea. A 2026 Science paper titled ‘ Wildfire damages and the cost-effective role of forest fuel treatments ’ by Frederik Strabo, Calvin Bryan and Matthew Reimer studied 285 large wildfires across 11 Western States between 2017 and 2023. Each of those fires burned into at least US Forest Service fuel treatment. The team estimated that treatments like thinning and prescribed burns cut the total area burned by 36% compared with what would have burned without them. For every dollar spent, the expected benefits were about $3.73.While the study doesn't look at the Cottonwood Fire, it shows why preparation is important.Climate adds another layer. In a 2016 study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences , John Abatzoglou and A. Park Williams found that human-caused climate change drove about 55% of the increase in fuel dryness from 1979 to 2015. By their estimates, climate change added about 4.2 million hectares of burned forest between 1984 and 2015, nearly doubling the total that would have been expected without it. Abatzoglou and Williams also say natural climate fluctuations play a role. The study looked at western forests as a whole and predated the fire, so it doesn't address the Cottonwood Fire.The Cottonwood Fire shows how quickly a green landscape can change. Satellites now help scientists and firefighters track fires in real time, which can help crews plan their response. Research also shows that taking care of forests before the fire begins can lessen the damage. Hot and dry conditions can raise the risk, and early preparation can really make a difference in saving a forest.
Article Summary: Landsat 8 and Landsat 9 satellites took images of the same section of Utah on 5 June and 29 June 2026. In these false-colour images, unburned vegetation appears bright green. The first image is of mountains that hadn’t been burned yet. Second shows a large brown scar across most of the picture.

Article Title: In 2024, Melinda French Gates gave 12 leaders $20 million each to distribute; a November 18 report says nearly all $240 million has been given out, with 91% of grants going to groups new to Pivotal
Article Text:
Melinda French GatesPhoto credit: AP Photo/Christophe Ena, File

How the programme worked

What the money has funded

How leaders used their funds

Ardern’s focus on maternal health

Former Prime Minister of New Zealand Jacinda Ardern Photo credit: AP Photo/Bruna Prado, File

A model for trust based giving

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

What comes next

In 2024, Melinda French Gates gave 12 leaders $20 million each to distribute through her philanthropic organisation Pivotal, with no strings attached beyond a deadline of the end of 2026. A November 18 report by The Associated Press (AP) says nearly all of the $240 million has now been given out, with 91 percent of the grants going to groups that had never received Pivotal funding before.The Global Leaders programme was part of French Gates’ broader plan to donate $1 billion to support women and girls. Its early results suggest that giving trusted figures freedom to direct large sums can reach organisations that traditional funders may overlook. Read more about it, as per the report, here:French Gates launched the Global Leaders programme in 2024 through Pivotal. She gave $20 million to each of 12 leaders, including psychologist Alfiee Breland-Noble, former New Zealand prime minister Jacinda Ardern, athlete Allyson Felix, and Afghan educator Shabana Basij-Rasikh. The only requirement was that the money be donated by the end of 2026. Beyond that, the leaders had freedom to decide which organisations or causes to support, as per AP and NPR.The programme was designed to expand who gets to make funding decisions.French Gates said the goal was to partner with experts whose firsthand knowledge could broaden Pivotal’s perspective and deepen its impact.According to Pivotal, the average grant distributed by the Global Leaders was about $240,000. The organisation says 91 percent of the donations went to groups that had not previously received funding from Pivotal.That figure is significant because it suggests the programme reached beyond Pivotal’s usual network. Rather than concentrating money among familiar recipients, the leaders used their own knowledge and communities to identify organisations that needed support.The grants covered a wide range of issues. Some focused on mental health, others on maternal health, and others on gender equality and community support.Breland-Noble created The MATTIE Fund to distribute her $20 million. She supported established groups such as the Asian Mental Health Collective but also sought out smaller organisations through Google, LinkedIn, Instagram, and audiences at her speaking events.Her search led her to BackSpinz Music Academy in North Carolina, which trains young people to use their creativity, and Daddy Stroller Social Club, which helps new fathers deal with postpartum depression. Breland-Noble said the opportunity allowed her to help others in the same way she had been helped.Ardern took a different approach. She used her $20 million to build new solutions rather than making large gifts to established organisations.Ardern worked with the International Rescue Committee on a programme to prevent postpartum hemorrhaging for women in areas affected by war and other humanitarian crises. The resulting Safer Births in Crises Consortium now focuses on preventing maternal deaths in South Sudan, Burkina Faso, and Papua New Guinea.She said the work took time because she wanted to create something that might not have existed otherwise. The approach reflects a more hands on use of the funding rather than simply distributing grants.Ardern also noted that her donations coincided with cuts to international aid. She said that reality made the work more urgent and pushed her to think about how to advocate for restoring support.Gary Barker, founder and CEO of the Equimundo Center for Masculinities and Social Justice, used his $20 million to expand his work and attract other funders. He launched the Caring Masculinity Fund to distribute the money.Barker said the experience changed how he approaches fundraising. He said he no longer wants to return to piecemeal fundraising and hopes to build similar relationships with other funders.The programme’s early results suggest that trust based philanthropy can work. By giving leaders freedom to direct large sums, Pivotal was able to reach organisations that might not have received funding otherwise.Pivotal says a final report on the Global Leaders programme will come next year. The organisation is already looking for ways to build on the model and encourage other donors to do the same.Haven Ley, Pivotal’s chief strategy officer, said the programme was not just about impact. He said it was also about testing a model that the organisation found intriguing.French Gates said the different vantage points on the world’s challenges made Pivotal more responsive and helped the Global Leaders be more impactful. The results so far suggest that approach may have lasting value.
Article Summary: In 2024, Melinda French Gates gave 12 leaders $20 million each to distribute through her philanthropic organisation Pivotal. The only requirement was that the money be donated by the end of 2026. A November 18 report by The Associated Press says nearly all of the $240 million has now been given out, with 91 percent of the grants going to groups that had never received Pvotal funding before.

Article Title: At 15, John Schnatter learned to make pizza while washing dishes; in 1984, he opened a shop in his father’s tavern with $1,600 in used equipment, building a chain that later topped 5,000 restaurants
Article Text:
John Schnatter began his famous Papa John's pizza business in 1984 at the back of his father’s tavern in Jeffersonville, Indiana. Image Credits: @thepapajohnschnatter/Instagram and Wikimedia Commons

What the dish sink taught him

Schnatter making pizza in the early days. Image Credits: @thepapajohnschnatter/Instagram

A tavern, a broom closet, and a big sacrifice

From a single shop to thousands

What universities saw in his story

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A dishwashing job gave John Schnatter something more useful than a pay cheque: a business idea. According to Entrepreneur, Schnatter was 15 years old washing dishes at a pizza restaurant called Rocky’s in Jeffersonville, Indiana. When the kitchen got busy, they pulled him over to make pizza. He paid attention. That habit led to a small shop in 1984 and later a chain of more than 5,000 restaurants.What Rocky’s taught Schnatter was a very simple lesson. The pizza station was right next to the dish sink, so he could see every plate that came back there. The magazine adds that he learned what the customers wanted. A clean plate meant that the pizza was perfect, and a plate with a half-eaten slice meant that it wasn't. There was also a gap he recognised. The national chains offered delivery service, while local businesses that made better quality food did not. That ended up becoming his business idea: make good quality pizza and bring it to the door. It wasn't a difficult idea; it came from what he saw working in a real kitchen.After graduating from Ball State University, Schnatter returned home.Mick’s Lounge, his father's tavern, was short on money. He sold the Camaro he loved to keep it going. Once the tavern was more stable, he bought $1,600 worth of used restaurant equipment, and then he began making pizza in a broom closet in the back. Papa John's 2007 filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission shows it started in 1984 in his dad's Jeffersonville tavern with $1,600 worth of used equipment. Schnatter recalls selling $5 pizzas from the back and 50-cent beers from the front. He said that his first goal was to make $50,000 a year and have $50,000 in the bank so he could get a date. Years later, he paid $250,000 to buy back the Camaro he had sold. He refers to it as a daily reminder that hard work and sacrifice pay off in the long run.The first proper Papa John's was opened near the tavern. Schnatter said it earned about $9,000 per week in sales, whereas other national franchises earned about $6,000. These were his own numbers. He has mentioned that he believed at age 22 that if he could beat them in one store, he could beat them anywhere. KFC and Long John Silver’s were rapidly expanding through franchising in the region. He chose the same route, saying it was instinctive. USF News reports that the 100th Papa John's was opened in Clarksville, Tennessee, seven years after he started selling pizzas in Mick's Lounge in 1984. As of May 2007, according to the company's filing, Papa John's operated more than 3,000 restaurants in 50 states and 29 countries.Later, universities found his story. In 2015, Ball State University announced that Schnatter would deliver the spring commencement address on 2 May and receive an honorary Doctor of Laws degree. Paul W. Ferguson, the university’s president, said Schnatter would inspire the audience with his story of hardwork, perseverance, and willingness to take risks.Ball State’s business college also presented him with an award of achievement in 1993 and a spot in its Hall of Fame in 2004. It said Papa John's had more than 4,600 stores in all 50 states and 34 countries at the time. USF News, reporting on a 2016 talk, adds more. Schnatter had always dreamed of selling pizza and almost quit college to open a franchise of another chain. Papa John's third-quarter 2026 results , released on 5 November 2026, counted 5,969 restaurants in 51 countries and territories as of 27 September 2026. That’s a dramatic turn for a business that began in a broom closet. His advice to young people remains simple: “Find something you love to do and something you’re good at.”
Article Summary: John Schnatter began his Papa John's pizza business in 1984 at the back of his father’s tavern in Jeffersonville, Indiana. The pizza station was right next to the dish sink, so he could see every plate that came back there. His advice to young people remains simple: “Find something you love to do and you’re good at it”

Article Title: In 2023 Caltech scientists beamed a microwave signal from a satellite in orbit to a rooftop on Earth; the experiment demonstrated wireless power transmission from space
Article Text:
AI Representation: Caltech scientists beamed solar power down from a satellite in orbit to a rooftop on Earth. Image credits: Chatgpt

Caltech launched its solar power demonstrator in January 2023

MAPLE transmitted power inside the spacecraft and towards Earth

NASA solar power satellite concepts. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Why collect solar energy in space?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

For years, scientists have explored whether satellites could collect sunlight in space and send the energy wirelessly to Earth. In 2023, researchers at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech) tested an important part of that area. Solar energy was harvested by their spacecraft and turned into electrical energy, which was then transferred to Earth using a microwave beam. They also had an energy receiver set up on the roof of a laboratory building in Pasadena that would receive the beam. The experiment proved that there was a way to get energy from space using a prototype, but the energy could not be used for any practical purpose.The SSPD-1 satellite, developed by Caltech, launched on January 3, 2023, on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket as part of the Transporter-6 rideshare mission, according to Caltech. It was carried to orbit aboard Momentus’s Vigoride-5 orbital transfer vehicle, which hosted three experimental payloads for a future solar power station. The first payload was MAPLE (Microwave Array for Power-transfer Low-orbit Experiment). It was created by the research team led by Caltech’s professor Ali Hajimiri. The MAPLE technology transmitter operated using custom-built chips. They enabled power transfer without any mechanical movement of the elements.DOLCE was used for testing the lightweight expandable space structure. ALBA had 32 types of photovoltaic cells.According to Caltech, MAPLE first achieved wireless power transmission on March 3, 2023. MAPLE transmitted microwave energy to two receiving arrays situated roughly a foot apart within the craft. The energy was then transformed into direct current electricity, which powered two small light-emitting diodes. The timing of the signals from MAPLE’s transmitter made the electromagnetic waves interfere constructively, forming a beam that could be steered electronically in the desired direction.According to Caltech, receiving equipment on the roof of the Gordon and Betty Moore Laboratory of Engineering in Pasadena picked up a microwave signal from the spacecraft on May 22, 2023. The signal arrived at the expected time and frequency and the frequency shifted just as the researchers had predicted from the Doppler effect caused by the satellite’s motion in orbit. Caltech announced the result on June 1, 2023. The detected power was not enough for practical electricity generation, but it confirmed that MAPLE could transmit a signal from orbit and that researchers could detect it on the ground.Solar cells on Earth need light as well as good weather conditions. In the designs Caltech envisions, a solar power system in space would not be affected by nighttime, seasons or clouds. The SSPD-1 demonstrator itself flew in low-Earth orbit, where it regularly passes through Earth’s shadow. Caltech’s future perspective is based on spacecraft that gather sunlight, convert it to electricity and send microwaves to the receiver on Earth.MAPLE experiments continued for eight months after the initial demonstrations, according to Caltech. Caltech later stated that some transmitter elements were subject to failure under stress conditions, resulting in the reduction of transmission power.In its January 16, 2024, mission report , Caltech described the mission’s successes and technical lessons. Commercial-scale solar power from space remains a future goal. The 2023 prototype was not built to generate electricity for homes or businesses, but the experiment showed that it could transmit microwave power from orbit and direct a detectable signal toward Earth.
Article Summary: Caltech launched its solar power demonstrator in January 2023. MAPLE transmitted power inside the spacecraft and towards Earth. The experiment proved that there was a way to get energy from space using a prototype, but the energy could not be used for any practical purpose.

Article Title: California’s Salton Sea has a new conservancy and more than $500 million committed to restoration projects as dust spreads; it still shelters more than 400 bird species on the Pacific Flyway
Article Text:
The Salton Sea in northeastern California. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

A shrinking lake leaves more exposed lake bed

Snow geese with Rock Hill in the background at Salton Sea National Wildlife Refuge. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Restoration projects are taking shape

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Construction of East Pond Expansion filled with water on May 22, 2025

As stated in the Salton Sea Program, California’s Salton Sea is facing an environmental challenge that affects both wildlife and nearby communities. As water levels fall, more of the lakebed is left exposed, allowing wind to carry dust into the surrounding areas and raising concerns about air quality. The shrinking water body also faces rising salinity and declining habitat conditions, putting pressure on the fish and other wildlife that depend on it. Despite these problems, the Salton Sea remains an important habitat along the Pacific Flyway, a major north-south migration corridor along western North America.According to Audubon, more than 400 bird species rely on the sea as habitat. The existing wetlands and open water in the sea are used by both resident and migratory birds as a place to feed and rest. This makes restoration essential not only for the welfare of wildlife, but also for the communities living near the area. According to California’s Governor's Office, to date, California has made a commitment worth more than $500 million in state and federal funding for the restoration and management of the Salton Sea. In April 2026, California launched the Salton Sea Conservancy, a state agency that will operate and maintain the restoration projects the Salton Sea Management Program completes, according to the Salton Sea Program The Salton Sea, located in southeastern California, is the state’s largest lake. There has been a reduction in the volume of water due to less drainage into the lake from agricultural activities. As the water volume decreases, there is an increase in salinity and exposure of the lakebed. When there are winds blowing over the exposed land area, the particles of dust are raised up and become part of the air pollution problem in the surrounding areas.But despite all these difficulties, the Salton Sea continues to be an important stopover point on the Pacific Flyway, which runs from North to South across Western North America. According to Audubon, over 400 types of birds rely on the lake for their habitat. It becomes an important aspect of the restoration plan to conserve what little habitat is left.California established the Salton Sea Management Program in 2018 as a 10-year plan for habitat restoration and dust suppression on exposed lakebed. By April 2026, the state had secured more than $500 million in combined state and federal funding for the program, according to the Governor’s Office, as reported by the Imperial Valley Press. The funding is meant for a wide range of activities but not necessarily construction of one project.One of these projects is the Species Conservation Habitat Project. It involves ponds, berms, nests and loafing islands, together with water delivery systems to benefit the fish and birds while creating shallow water habitat on exposed lakebed. California expects that the project will cover over 9000 acres upon completion.The conservancy is designed to operate and maintain restoration projects once they are built. They are responsible for operating and maintaining those projects, coordinating with public agencies and engaging local communities. This organisation controls the land and water rights necessary for the restoration projects. The future of Salton Sea depends not only on constructing but also on managing these projects. Habitat restoration, dust separation and management of completed projects will all require constant effort. This organisation provides the State of California with such an opportunity.
Article Summary: California’s Salton Sea is facing an environmental challenge that affects both wildlife and nearby communities. As water levels fall, more of the lakebed is left exposed, allowing wind to carry dust into the surrounding areas and raising concerns about air quality. The shrinking water body also faces rising salinity and declining habitat conditions, putting pressure on the fish and other wildlife that depend on it.

Article Title: In 2007, a Connecticut family preserved flowers from a garden a father had grown with his daughter; their seeds later helped launch a community project across the state
Article Text:
Mirabilis jalapa in the botanical garden of the University of Latvia. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Family members saved the four-o’clocks

The flowers became Connecticut’s Children’s State Flower

Connecticut community garden. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A father-daughter tradition continues in gardens

A garden in Cheshire, Connecticut, became the starting point for a project that would spread flowers across the street. According to the Connecticut Secretary of the State , the plants were four-o’clocks, grown each year by 11-year-old Michaela Petit and her father, William. After tragedy struck their family in 2007, relatives preserved the flowers. Seeds from them later helped form Michaela’s Garden Project and the flower was eventually recognised as Connecticut’s State Children’s Flower. In July 2007, Michaela, her mother, Jennifer Hawke-Petit and her older sister, Hayley, were killed in a home invasion at their Cheshire home, according to NBC Connecticut . Michaela was just 11 years old then. The garden continued to be a symbol of the time she spent with her father, planting and tending flowers.Following the incident, the four-o’clock plants were moved out of the Cheshire garden by members of her family. The plants survived and flowered successfully, producing seeds. The seeds became the initial phase for Michaela‘s Garden Project, an attempt made to motivate children to be involved in service to the community. It provided schools, volunteers and community organisations with an opportunity to honour the memory of Michaela by cultivating the same type of flowers that she planted along with her father.It helped to spread the plants and gardens all over Connecticut, as well as associate gardens with service. It offered children a chance to cooperate in working with flowers. According to the Royal Horticultural Society, the flowers are Mirabilis jalapa, a bushy, tuberous perennial from tropical America. The blossoms are very fragrant and come in colours such as pink, red, yellow and white. The name four-o’clock is derived from the time when flowers start blooming, usually in the late afternoon, at about four-o’clock.The project had expanded to become more than just the initial family garden project. Volunteers made sure that Michaela’s four-o’clock flowers were planted in various gardens within the state. Being associated with Michaela and the community effort to promote them, there was a suggestion to honour the flowers officially. In 2015, Connecticut designated Michaela Petit’s four-o’clock as its State Children’s Flower under Public Act 15-77.The state's official account explains that the flowers were named in her memory and originated from the plants she and her father had grown together in Cheshire. It also describes how family members transplanted the flowers after her death and how the seeds helped create the garden project. Connecticut has its own designated state flower, which is the mountain laurel. The State Children’s Flower acknowledges Michaela’s four-o’clock as well as the initiative around it.This does not mean that the mountain laurel will be substituted for another state flower.The process of transporting the flowers from a single family garden to other gardens in Connecticut started with the preservation of those flowers. Plants associated with memories of Michaela and her father were preserved as seeds in order to offer other people the chance to participate in the project and grow the flowers. Four-o’clock has remained connected to the memory of Michaela and the spirit of community effort that came from her garden. The flowers tell the tale of the involvement of children and serving their communities through gardening. New gardens developed out of the ongoing efforts of the project, with Michaela Patit’s four-o’clocks.
Article Summary: Michaela Petit, 11, and her father, William, were killed in a home invasion in 2007. Family members preserved the four-o'clocks and planted them in a garden in Cheshire, Connecticut. The plants survived and flowered successfully, producing seeds. The seeds became the initial phase for Michaela’s Garden Project, an attempt made to motivate children to be involved in service to the community.

Article Title: In 1986, Ted and Ruth Baum bought a Joan Mitchell painting for $65,000; on November 16, 2026, the same artwork sold at Sotheby's in New York for $19.3 million, nearly 300 times its original price

Joan Mitchell painting leads the Baum collection auction

A collection valued at more than $100 million

The Baums' journey as art collectors

A legacy extending beyond the auction room

An artwork purchased for $65,000 four decades ago has now fetched more than $19 million at auction, offering a striking illustration of how artistic vision, collecting instincts and time can transform the value of a painting. Joan Mitchell’s Green Book of Barbara Guest (1960), once acquired by American collectors Ted and Ruth Baum, emerged as the star attraction at Sotheby’s in New York on November 16, 2026. The painting sold for approximately $19.31 million, almost 300 times its original purchase price, becoming the headline lot in a landmark auction dedicated to the couple’s extensive art collection.The sale took place as part of Sotheby’s Vision: The Extraordinary Collection of Theodore and Ruth Baum Evening Auction. According to Heni News, the Mitchell painting achieved a price 60 per cent above its $12 million low estimate. The work also carried a guarantee, providing a level of financial security ahead of the auction.Its remarkable performance underscored the continued appeal of Mitchell's work in the international art market. The painting had previously changed hands twice before reaching the auction block as part of the Baum collection.Another notable result came from Roy Lichtenstein’s Two Paintings: Sleeping Muse (Study) (1983), which sold for $3.78 million against a low estimate of $1.5 million. Heni News reported that the work, also backed by a guarantee, had been traded eight times previously.The Mitchell painting was among more than 130 works assembled by Ted and Ruth Baum, whose collection is estimated to exceed $100 million. As reported by The Art Insider and ARTnews, Sotheby's is presenting the collection through multiple auctions rather than offering it all at once.Around two dozen works featured in the November 16 evening sale, with additional pieces scheduled for a November 17 day auction. The remaining works will appear in different Sotheby's sales over the following year, although their final number and individual estimates have not yet been disclosed, the report adds.Before the auction, Rothko and Ruscha works were among the leading lots, each carrying estimates of $10 million to $15 million. Mitchell's painting was valued at approximately $12 million, while works by Burri, Fontana and Warhol were estimated between $4 million and $6 million.Ted Baum, a pioneering figure in American cable television, and Ruth Baum, an interior designer, began building their collection in the 1970s. Their interest initially centred on modern drawings and watercolours, with purchases including works by Fernand Léger and Pablo Picasso.According to ARTnews, their collecting ambitions evolved significantly in 1983, when they acquired an untitled 1967 Rothko painting on paper featuring red and orange tones. The purchase marked a turning point towards contemporary art and eventually led them to artists such as Mitchell, Sam Francis, Hans Hofmann, Lichtenstein and Wesselmann.Their later acquisitions reflected an equally strong interest in European abstraction. These included Lucio Fontana's Concetto Spaziale, Attese (1960), purchased at Sotheby's London in 2000, and Warhol's The Scream (After Edvard Munch) (1984), acquired in 2006.The Baums' influence extended well beyond collecting. They supported cultural institutions and philanthropic initiatives across the communities where they lived, including New York, New Jersey, Southampton and Palm Beach.The Norton Museum of Art in West Palm Beach houses the Ruth and Theodore Baum Gallery, which displays part of their collection. The couple also supported the museum's contemporary art programme and contributed works by artists including Dale Chihuly and Leo Villareal. They were additionally associated with New York's Guggenheim Museum and the Parrish Art Museum.Ted Baum died in 2021, while Ruth Baum passed away in 2026, just months before the collection's major auction presentation.As part of the sale, Sotheby's is also taking selected highlights on an international exhibition tour, with presentations planned in London, Hong Kong, Los Angeles, Paris and New York, as reported by The Art Insider and ARTnews.The $19.3 million Mitchell result is therefore more than an exceptional auction achievement. It offers a glimpse into the legacy of two collectors whose decades-long commitment to art has now become part of the market's history.Images Courtesy: Sothebys, The Art Insider, and Joan Mitchell Foundation
Article Summary: Joan Mitchell's Green Book of Barbara Guest (1960) sold for $19.31 million at Sotheby's in New York on November 16, 2026. The painting was among more than 130 works assembled by American collectors Ted and Ruth Baum, whose collection is estimated to exceed $100 million. The Baums' influence extended well beyond collecting, with the couple supporting cultural institutions and philanthropic initiatives.
